title: Pai Gow Poker in Canada: Rules, Odds and Strategy
excerpt: Pai Gow Poker is the slowest, gentlest game on the casino floor. Here are the rules, the house edge, and the setting strategy Canadian players should use.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
If you want your bankroll to last an entire evening, Pai Gow Poker is the game to learn. It is the slowest-moving table game most Canadian casinos offer, it pushes an extraordinary number of hands, and a competent player faces a house edge that compares well with almost anything else on the floor. It is also badly misunderstood — most players who sit down have no idea that the way they arrange their cards is a strategic decision worth real money over time.

The game is a hybrid: American poker hand rankings grafted onto the Chinese domino game pai gow. It arrived in Canadian casinos decades ago and has since become a fixture at online tables too, where the pace is entirely under your control. This guide covers how a hand actually plays out, what the numbers look like, and the setting rules that separate a break-even session from a slow bleed.

How a hand of Pai Gow Poker works

You are dealt seven cards from a 53-card deck — a standard deck plus one joker. Your job is to split those seven cards into two hands: a five-card hand (called the high hand or the back) and a two-card hand (the low hand or the front). You then compare both hands against the dealer's two hands.

The critical rule is that your five-card hand must rank higher than your two-card hand. Set them the other way around and the hand is a foul, and you lose automatically. Because your two-card hand can be at best a pair of aces, the strongest realistic front hand is limited, and that constraint drives almost every strategic decision in the game.

Settlement is simple:

  • You win both comparisons: your bet pays even money, minus the house commission.
  • You lose both comparisons: you lose your stake.
  • You win one and lose one: the hand is a push and your stake is returned.
  • A tie in either comparison goes to the dealer — this is the built-in house advantage.

That third outcome is what makes Pai Gow Poker feel so different from other table games. Roughly 40% of hands end in a push. You can play for two hours and finish within a few dollars of where you started, which is either deeply relaxing or deeply boring depending on temperament.

The joker and the commission

The joker is partially wild. It can complete a straight or a flush, and it can act as an ace. It cannot be used freely as any card you like, which trips up players who assume it functions like a wild card in home games.

The commission is the other detail newcomers miss. Winning hands are typically charged a 5% commission by the house. Some online tables use a commission-free variant instead, where certain dealer hands push rather than lose. Neither is automatically better — the commission-free versions compensate elsewhere — but you should know which version you are sitting at before you play.

The odds: what edge are you actually facing?

Played with reasonable strategy and standard 5% commission, the house edge on the main bet sits in the region of 2.5% to 2.8% of the amount wagered. On paper that is worse than basic-strategy blackjack, which is closer to half a percent. But the raw percentage understates how gentle the game is in practice.

Two things soften it. First, the push rate means far less money actually changes hands per round. Second, the game is slow — perhaps 25 to 30 hands an hour at a live table, versus double or triple that at a fast blackjack game. Your expected hourly loss, which is what actually matters to your bankroll, is often lower at Pai Gow than at games with a better headline edge.

Playing as the banker, where the rules allow it, flips some of the edge in your favour because ties then go to you. It also requires a larger bankroll, since as banker you cover other players' bets. Online, banking rotation rules vary considerably between platforms, so read the specific table rules before assuming it is available.

Setting strategy: the decisions that matter

Every seven-card deal can be arranged many ways, and the difference between the best and worst arrangement is significant. The guiding principle is balance. A monstrous five-card hand paired with a garbage two-card hand wins one comparison and loses the other — a push, which pays nothing. You want both hands strong enough to have a genuine chance.

Some reliable default rules:

  • No pair: put the highest card in the back and the next two highest in the front.
  • One pair: keep the pair in the back and send your two highest remaining cards to the front.
  • Two pairs: usually split them — the higher pair in the back, the lower pair in the front. The main exception is when the higher pair is very strong and your remaining cards include an ace, where keeping both pairs together can be better.
  • Three pairs: always put the highest pair in the front and play the other two pairs in the back.
  • A straight or flush: play it in the back only if you can still put a decent pair or two high cards in front. Otherwise, break it.
  • Full house: nearly always split — the three of a kind in the back, the pair in the front.

Most online implementations offer a "house way" auto-set button that arranges your cards using the dealer's own rules. It is not optimal, but it is close, and it is far better than guessing. If you are learning, use it as a training wheel and compare its choices against the rules above until the patterns become automatic.

Side bets and where to play in Canada

Almost every Pai Gow table offers a bonus side bet paying on premium seven-card hands. As with side bets across the casino floor, the house edge on these is dramatically higher than on the main game — often in the double digits. They exist to sell excitement to a game that is deliberately unexciting. If you enjoy the occasional flutter, keep the stakes small and treat the cost as entertainment rather than strategy.

Pai Gow is not stocked as widely as slots or blackjack, so table availability varies by operator. Is it worth your time?

Pai Gow Poker rewards a specific kind of player: someone who values session length over swings, who enjoys a decision on every hand, and who does not need frequent wins to stay engaged. If you want variance and big scores, slots will serve you better. If you want to sit with a modest bankroll for an hour, make genuine strategic choices, and walk away close to even more often than not, few games do it better.
